newsitem.title: USA: Fund company chiefs warn of over-exuberance.
newsitem.headline: Fund company chiefs warn of over-exuberance.

text.p: Mutual fund company executives said Thursday that the media and even their own ads feed unrealistic investor expectations, but fundholders have proved to be remarkably adept.
"I actually think that investors have been remarkably well behaved," John Brennan, chief executive of Vanguard Group Inc said on a panel discussion.
Even investments in small company funds have not suffered from redemptions despite their laggard gains behind the large company funds over the past year.
"The same people (the media) who are worrying correctly about investor expectations are nurturing them," he said.
The problem arises when all the hype over the short-term gains of a few well-performing mutual funds causes investors to abandon their long-term goals, Lasser said.
Studies have shown that trying to time the markets and reap the best returns actually cost investors, said Arthur Zeikel, chief executive of Merrill Lynch Asset Management.
The growth of mutual fund supermarkets which allow investors to trade funds from a variety of companies may shorten investors' time horizons, Lasser said.
"The supermarkets encourage trading and that's not what most of us think mutual funds are for," Lasser said.
However, the fund industry's own ads which brag about the number of stars awarded by the independent fund rating agency Morningstar may also spur trading, Zeikel said.
"Stars have become the differentiation," he said. "It's a mark of distinction to have them."

On the other hand, the industry has repeatedly warned investors in newsletters sent to shareholders to be cautious and not to expect the roughly 17 percent annual growth in stocks since 1982 to continue, Brennan said.
However, all the nay-sayers who have warned about a stock market correction over the past couple of years have been premature or wrong, Zeikel said.

"The problem we face is that the message is still sound, but the listener has to a large extent been turned off," he said. "We have to recognize that telling people there's a 100-year flood, they think they have 99 years to go," he added.
"Frankly, I'm surprised but I'm encouraged by that as well," Brennan said at the annual meeting of the mutual fund industry group Investment Company Institute in Washington.

But while many investors have learned the benefits of long-term, systematic investing rather than trying to time the market, the continued runup in stock prices has undermined those lessons, the panelists said.

The same publications which warn of over-exuberance in the market also tout the hottest funds and the best-performing portfolio managers, said Lawrence Lasser, chief executive of Putnam Investments Inc.
